title: Failure to Reasonably Accommodate Religious Beliefs Snares Wildlife Department, Nets Win for Employees (US) - The National Law Review

A recent decision from the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit—Cherry et al. v Washington Dep’t of Fish & Wildlife, et al., is a primer in employer obligations when reasonably accommodating employees’ religious beliefs. In August 2021, the Governor of Washington mandated that nearly all State employees vaccinate against COVID-19 or face termination. Five Washington Fish & Wildlife Department employees sought exemption on religious grounds. Although the Department agreed their requests stemmed from their sincerely held religious beliefs, it nonetheless maintained that vaccination was required if they wished to remain in their current roles, which required work “in the physical presence of others.” All five employees offered to mask-and-distance, and some suggested telework. All employees also expressed interest in transferring to another job that would eliminate their religious conflict. The Department replied that “reassignment remains a possibility, although opportunity may be limited,” then directed the employees to speak to a Reasonable Accommodation Specialist. However, when one of the employees approached the Reasonable Accommodation Specialist, she claimed “[t]here’s just nothing available.” None of the five employees completed the reassignment application process, which they described as “a show.” Their impressions were not off base; out of 122 requests for religious accommodation reassignments, the Department only granted 17, and the data suggested that reassignment, when it was available, often was not to a comparable position. All five employees were ultimately fired. Because the employees did not complete the reassignment process, the district court dismissed their religious discrimination claims, but the Ninth Circuit reversed. The appellate court concluded that merely offering the reassignment process was not, by itself, an offer of reasonable accommodation. Instead, presenting an alternative position or arrangement that would have eliminated the asserted conflict between the employee’s religious beliefs and their current job was the required first step in the accommodation process. From there, the parties could have discussed the reasonableness of the offered accommodation or other alternatives, but since the Department’s offer “was nothing more than an opportunity for reassignment, couched in language that made success appear unlikely,” the court was unable to conclude as a matter of law that the Department had made a good faith effort to reasonably accommodate the employees’ religious beliefs. The decision highlights a common employer mistake, which is conflating the interactive process required by the Americans with Disabilities Act with the religious accommodation requirement under Title VII. The Department argued that it had opened an opportunity for an interactive dialogue when it informed the employees about the process for applying for reassignment. The Ninth Circuit dismissed this argument, emphasizing that the employer’s duty in a religious accommodation setting requires first proposing a specific accommodation, which in this case would have required offering “concrete options for transfer.” It was not enough just to propose the possibility of transfer. The distinction is subtle, but enough in this case to warrant remand for trial. Employers should not assume from the decision that all vaccine mandates were impermissible, or that reassignment is always required when an employee requests religious accommodation. Instead, what employers should take from the decision is that their duty to reasonably accommodate employees’ religious beliefs imposes a duty to present a concrete accommodation proposal, and then to work in good faith to determine whether the accommodation eliminates the employee’s religious conflict without imposing an undue burden on the business. Perfunctory gestures will not suffice. The friendship between BTS (BTS) and actor Song Kang during their military service has drawn attention. Song Kang revealed on the web variety show 'Salon Drop' on the YouTube channel 'TEO TEO', released on the 25th, that he built a close bond with V while serving in the same military unit. When Jang Do-yeon mentioned four-cut photos taken by V and Song Kang during their service and asked how they became friends, Song Kang explained, "We became close in the military. title: Walter V. Klemp Discloses Investment at Moleculin Biotech with 9.87% Stake - TradingView
content: Walter V. Klemp, Chairman, CEO and President of Moleculin Biotech, Inc., disclosed a 9.87% stake in the company’s common stock. He filed the Schedule 13D on Aug. 25, 2026, after buying shares and warrants in an Aug. 3, 2026 public offering. The move highlights insider buying and includes warrant terms that cap his ownership unless he elects a higher limit. Klemp bought the shares and Series I warrants for investment and can adjust his position over time. The warrants include a limit that blocks exercises above certain ownership levels; he has already elected to "increase that limitation to 9.99%," effective Oct. 18, 2026. As CEO and board chair, Klemp helped approve proposals in the Aug. 24, 2026 proxy, including director elections, more shares for the 2024 equity plan, removal of select supermajority votes, and a potential reverse split. He also notes he may buy more or sell shares in the future and could consider strategic transactions if circumstances warrant. Walter V. For much of the game, the All Blacks were less assured in their decision-making, and that was down to the Lions taking the game to them and scoring five tries that were all converted by their deadeye first five-eighths Chris Smit, two of them in the first six minutes. Flanker Siba Mahashe was effective with the ball in hand while halfback Nico Steyn was a constant in his control from the base of scrums and rucks. For the All Blacks, flanker Ethan Blackadder made a massive contribution towards keeping his side in the game with two tries and strong carries complementing his turnover plays and tackles. The performance of centre Rieko Ioane, who scored two key tries, helped turn around a 17-35 deficit and set up a stronger run from home. And when Lakai, prop Xavier Numia and lock Jamie Hannah joined the action, there was a noticeable lift in the continuity play that carried the All Blacks home. For first five-eighths Richie Mo’unga, it was a workmanlike return, with some of his trademark runs at the opposition but less influential than when in his prime. Six minutes of early embarrassment for the All Blacks saw the Lions two tries up, and helped them to a 21-17 lead at halftime. The Lions raced out with their big pack charging onto the ball at pace to test the All Blacks’ defence from the outset. Then, from a fifth-minute lineout, it was lively halfback Nico Steyn who pierced the defence when breaking from a ruck to score under the posts. The home team cleared the restart to touch. The All Blacks claimed the lineout, but halfback Noah Hotham’s pass was intercepted by barnstorming Lions blindside flanker Siba Mahashe, who intercepted the ball and ran 35 metres to score. It reflected a disjointed All Blacks effort, with mistakes and penalties mounting. However, the All Blacks responded and but for a last pass, a forward pass from flanker Wallace Sititi to wing Fehi Fineanganofo, a minute from the break, after some magic from Beauden Barrett, who dropped a high pass to his right hand with control to his left foot to kick ahead, they would have taken the lead for the first time. Hotham had almost immediate relief from the intercept when wing Emoni Narawa ran from the base of a ruck to beat two defenders before slipping the ball to the unmarked Hotham for a 10th-minute try. Narawa, who enjoyed plenty of ball in hand in the free-flowing game, was in the action again in the 24th minute when the All Blacks ran the ball from their line through second five-eighths Timoci Tavatavanawai and Fineanganofo, initially. The ball was moved across the field where Barrett’s backhand pass was moved on perfectly by captain and lock Patrick Tuipuloto to Narawa, who scored. A clever break and kick ahead by home fullback Quan Horn gave the Lions momentum that saw them strike deep into All Blacks territory with good ball control before Steyn ran across the front of the All Blacks’ defence before popping a pass to wing Kelly Mpeku, who dived in at the corner after 32 minutes. But three minutes later from the restart, the All Blacks utilised a quick lineout throw by Barrett, and a thrilling counter-attack with the ball passed perfectly through player after player before flanker Ethan Blackadder capped his hard-working first half with the try. However, if the Lions' first-half start was electric, their second half was nuclear as Smit put up a box kick, which was taken at speed by wing Erich Cronje. He linked with Mahashe, who charged down the line before dropping a pass to Cronje in support. He kicked the ball ahead and over the line to score a minute after the start. Then, the Lions got back into All Blacks’ territory and from a five-metre scrum in the 46th minute they pushed the All Blacks back for No8 Francke Horn to score. At 17-35 down, the All Blacks lifted the tempo, and it was Barrett, who passed out to Ioane, who cut through two defenders and raced 40m to score. Then, six minutes later, as the Lions looked to stretch their lead, Ioane picked off an errant midfield pass, and he ran 50 metres to get the All Blacks within four points. They claimed the lead for the first time after 61 minutes when, from a turnover in their territory, they moved the ball wide with a Mo’unga punch, resulting in him getting the ball to Ioane, who had moved to wing. He passed to Tavatavanawai, who had Blackadder inside him to take a pass and run in his second try. The win was finally sealed at full time when Narawa made the most of the All Blacks’ scrum power, which revealed itself in the last 10 minutes with two crucial scrums. The first got them out of their territory. It set them up for their final chance, which saw replacement No8 Peter Lakai take the ball into the goalmouth before it was sent through the line for Narawa, to cut back past four cover defenders to score his second try and secure the victory. Lions 35 (Nico Steyn, Siba Mahashe, Kelly Mpeku, Erich Cronje, Francke Horn tries; Chris Smit 5 con) All Blacks 41 (Noah Hotham, Emoni Narawa 2, Ethan Blackadder 2, Rieko Ioane 2 tries; Beauden Barrett con; Richie Mo’unga 2 con*)*. HT: 21-17

title: The Most Valuable Cards in Yu-Gi-Oh! Legendary Arc-V Decks - Beckett
content: Legendary Arc-V Decks arrived August 7, and three weeks of completed sales have sorted the box into two very different tiers. The guaranteed contents are cheap by design. Every copy ships with 3 Secret Rares, 18 Ultra Rares, and 144 Commons, and Legendary Decks products exist to flood the market with playable staples, so almost nothing in that guaranteed pool clears a few dollars. The money is in the bonus pack. Each of the three decks includes a 56th card drawn from a six-card pool, arriving as a Secret Rare with a chance to upgrade into a Starlight Rare instead, and those Starlight pulls are carrying the entire collector value of this release. Eighteen cards are eligible across the three decks, and the ones that have found a settled price are trading between roughly $50 and $100. The highest price in the set belongs to the Lunalight boss monster, one of the three cards Konami put on the box art alongside Odd-Eyes Arc Pendulum Dragon and Hi-Speedroid Kitedrake. Liger Dancer is a Level 12 Fusion with 3800 ATK and 3500 DEF that is unaffected by card effects other than Lunalight cards, attacks twice per Battle Phase, and can send a Lunalight monster from the Extra Deck to the graveyard to wipe every Special Summoned monster your opponent controls. Completed sales on the Starlight print are landing at roughly $98. The Common copy that ships in the Lunalight deck itself trades at closer to $5, meaning the identical card is worth roughly 20 times more depending on which slot of the box it came out of. *Buy Lunalight Liger Dancer cards on TCGPlayer or eBay The next highest confirmed price is not a boss monster or a nostalgia piece. It’s a Link-2 DARK Spellcaster with 1200 ATK, first printed in Dimension Force in 2022 and greeted on arrival as the successor to Electrumite, the Pendulum searcher the format had lost. Link Summon it to the Extra Monster Zone, pay 1200 Life Points, and it adds any Pendulum Monster from the deck to your hand, with the catch that you have to actually Pendulum Summon that turn or you lose access to your monster effects and your Pendulum Zone for the rest of it. Search power on that scale plus a Starlight print run is a reliable formula, and sales are settling in the $87 to $89 range depending on the source. The Common version out of the Odd-Eyes deck sits under $2. *Buy Beyond the Pendulum cards on TCGPlayer or eBay Black Sheep is the least imposing card on this list and one of the most important. A Level 2 DARK monster with 100 ATK, it does its work from the hand, discarding itself to either add a Lunalight monster from the graveyard or pull Polymerization straight out of the deck, then offering another recovery effect if it hits the graveyard as Fusion Material. It’s the card that makes the Lunalight opening hand function, which is why the Starlight print is drawing prices at roughly $65. Anyone opening this box will find ordinary copies for pocket change. *Buy Lunalight Black Sheep cards on TCGPlayer or eBay The Speedroid deck’s most valuable bonus pull carries the Stardust name and Yusei’s design language, though the card itself is a more recent addition, first hitting the TCG in 2022. Stardust Charge Warrior is a Level 6 WIND Synchro with 2000 ATK and 1300 DEF that draws a card the moment it’s Synchro Summoned and can attack every Special Summoned monster your opponent controls once each. It needs only 1 Tuner plus one or more non-Tuners, which is exactly the kind of open requirement a Speedroid deck can meet on demand. Sales on the Starlight print are running right around $50. The standard printing inside the Speedroid deck trades near $3. This card is a reminder that the bonus pool rewards recognizable reprints as readily as it does the set’s genuinely new cards. *Buy Stardust Charge Warrior cards on TCGPlayer or eBay Not every card holding value here is a lottery pull. For collectors buying this product to open rather than to chase a specific Starlight, Fuwalos is the one card worth pulling out of the pile on sight, and the only entry on this list that does not require winning a bonus pack lottery to hold. title: In Loving Memory of Phyllis V. Pavlich - KRTN
content:
Phyllis V. Pavlich entered the world on May 30, 1931. She was the 5th of 8 children born to Dragan “Charles” and Matilda “Tilda” (Starkovich) Pavlich. Her siblings were: Agnes, David, Joseph, Betty Jo, Mary Lou, Katherine, and James. Her early years were spent in the coal camp of Brilliant, NM. The family later moved from Brilliant to Raton, where they settled at the home on the east side of town which was to become known as the Farm. Phyllis graduated from St. Patrick Academy in Raton and went on to college at NM Highlands University in Las Vegas where she majored in Elementary Education. After graduation, she taught for a time at the coal camp of Colmor, then lived and taught for a number of years in California. She eventually returned to Raton where she accepted a position teaching junior high Girl’s Physical Education. Her stories associated with those years in the Raton schools were numerous and often hilarious. She worked the rest of her career in the Raton school system and eventually retired from there. After retirement, she continued to live in Raton assisting her mother and sister, Betty Jo. Phyllis was a long-time, active member of St. Joseph’s Catholic Church. She took a great deal of interest in and supported the parish’s various activities. Most days would find her at one point or another at her usual seat at daily Mass. Phyllis made sure that the Raton Farm was always open and welcoming to the many family members and friends who would stop in for a few days’ visit or simply on their way through the area. She made it a favorite place to stay. Phyllis was called from this world to be with her Lord and Savior on August 16, 2026. Though she never had any children of her own, Aunt Phyllis was a favorite of her many nieces and nephews. She took it upon herself to take most (if not all) of those nieces and nephews to Disneyland at some point. Often, she enlisted her sister May Lou (when she was available) in this effort – probably as much for her own sanity as for crowd control. Various aspects of those “vacations” still come up in discussions decades later – giving credence to the old expression that “You’ll laugh about this someday.” During her teaching years, Phyllis having the keys to the school’s swimming pool was a boon for the nieces and nephews and a way for us to burn off some energy while visiting the Farm. Also, taking the kids out in the field to fly kites or taking day trips up Cimarron Canyon or to Mt. Capulin were fun ways (at least for the kids) to keep the youngsters occupied. Phyllis’ years of teaching young girls had a long-reaching impact on multiple generations of women. To this day, there continue to be instances of women of widely varying ages in neighboring town and, yes, even neighboring states who, upon hearing the Pavlich name and discovering the connection to Phyllis, will comment along the lines of “ ’Pav’ taught me/my mother/my grandmother back in the day.” And their recollections of Phyllis and those times are uniformly fond and upbeat. To this day, when Phyllis tells of seeing or hearing about one of her former students, she still refers to them as “one of my little girls.” Phyllis had a pretty solid (some would say “rigid”) idea of what was right/wrong/fair/unfair and woe to those who crossed that line when it involved Phyllis and those around her. Just ask certain city council members, highway department officials, state regulators, and even a U.S. senator who found themselves (temporarily) on the wrong side of Phyllis’ fair/unfair divide until such time as they saw the light. Phyl also believed that family is one of the most important things in life – just behind faith in God and ahead (just barely) of her favorite sports teams. At the Farm, Phyl always made sure that a pot of coffee was ready for guests, and she continued Tilda’s tradition of constantly trying to get guests to eat something – anything. That was just the way it was going to be, so it was best to go with the flow. And while sitting around the kitchen table, pretty much any topic was fair game for discussion under the strictly enforced rule of “What is said in the kitchen stays in the kitchen!” Phyllis could be welcoming, caring, irritating, and maddening all at the same time; but you always knew that she loved you. And she was loved as well. Phyllis’ faith was unrelenting, and she put her trust in God and His mercy all throughout her life. She prayed fervently for all her family as well as a long list of “special attention” individuals each and every day (her prayer intentions box was always crammed full). Most of us were on that list at one time or another (some of us for much longer than others). Phyllis was absolutely faithful in her prayers for others; and now she can continue those prayers for all of us from a new vantage point. title: OMEGA Ticks Forward With Evolved Speedmaster 38mm Collection - V Magazine
content: The Swiss watchmaker continues shaping the industry with a sparkling extension of their 38mm watch line The Swiss watchmaker continues shaping the industry with a sparkling extension of their 38mm watch line Inspired by the many codes found in OMEGA’s legendary Moonwatch, the watchmaker has expanded its 38mm watch line, adding seven new interpretations to its illustrious catalogue. Each new design adds a refined feature to the line, as well as a refreshed color palette, bringing each piece closer and closer to it’s original reference. The new models vary starkly in material construction. From gold links to bezels set in diamonds, OMEGA’s latest showcase offers a sparkling diversity. Within the steel-on-steel selection,  silver, white, and black-dialed pieces, with the black most closely resembling the original Moonwatch, and the white and silver sporting colorfully varnished dials. Within the line are two additional bicolor models, one a silvery opaline tone, and the other an ivory “cappuccino.” The silver model features a stainless steel casing and an 18K Moonshine Gold bezel. For the ivory-toned piece, OMEGA also employed a gold bezel as well as a gold-linked bracelet. In the line’s top tier sit two diamond-encrusted pieces. Each bezel is encrusted with 52 diamonds, with one sporting an ice blue dial and the other polished with mother-of-pearl purity. Beyond the new palette and material construction, the watchmaker has employed new technology in their latest work. Straying from the Speedmaster’s previously oval subdials, the new collection features rounded subdials. The content on the dials has also been heavily pulled back, making the appearance of the dials more minimal and, thus, sporty. “The Speedmaster 38 mm has always taken its cues from the Moonwatch, while keeping size, colour, and simplicity in mind,” says Raynald Aeschlimann, President and CEO of OMEGA in a statement. “With this latest update, we’ve taken the Moonwatch inspiration even further, helping to enrich the Speedmaster DNA while still retaining the refined and unique nature that the 38 mm range is known for.” We are using cookies to give you the best experience on our website. title: Lions v All Blacks: Winners and losers as 'unplayable' wing scores two but veteran playmaker left 'frustrated' - Planet Rugby
content: The All Blacks squeezed past the Lions on Tuesday to continue their unbeaten tour of South Africa. The All Blacks squeezed past the Lions 41-35 on Tuesday to continue their unbeaten tour of South Africa. Here are our winners and losers from the game. Nico Steyn: He may be just 24, but he played like a man 10 years his senior. He led the Lions attack with confidence, controlling backs and forwards with military precision at a pace that more than matched their international opponents. In fact, his opening try put the All Blacks on the back foot from the opening minutes, then backed it up with a superb box-kick clearance from the restart. He showed real maturity to nudge the ball out of play as the clock turned red, bringing an end to a scintillating first half. He’s only ever played for South Africa’s A team, but with further performances like that, a full squad call-up cannot be far off. Siba Mahashe: He had the game of his life at 21. He made a brilliant interception from an early lineout, then showed excellent pace to race away from the covering All Black defence to score the Lions’ second try of the match. He later made a fantastic break down the left wing to set up the opening try of the second half, before later being right in the middle of the action as the Lions powered over from close range. Almost all of his actions were highlight-worthy, but his huge tackle on Samisoni Taukei’aho will make the cover reel. Emoni Narawa: The Chiefs winger was utterly unplayable at times. His early break down the right wing set the tone for the rest of his evening. He was not satisfied with the odd touch of the ball, but insisted on popping up all over the field. His tenacity resulted in a try midway through the first half, collecting the ball after a brilliant team move. Later, in the final moments of the game, he stepped five players to score in the corner to confirm the All Blacks’ victory. He’s seen limited club action this past season due to a foot injury, but this performance gave a solid indication that he is truly back to his best. Despite being heralded as somewhat of a ‘surprise inclusion’ in the tour squad, he’s certainly playing like he deserves a spot in the Test team. Rieko Ioane: The veteran All Black looked as though he didn’t have a care in the world, playing the sort of rugby that earned him international recognition many years ago. He exploited the Lions defence with pure pace, making 141 metres from just six carries, and showed excellent hands in the midfield to bring his teammates into the game. He stepped above the rest in the second half, showing unreal gas to score a brilliant solo try, just as the Lions were threatening to run away with the game. His defensive game cannot be understated either, making a team high of 10 tackles – although he did miss five. He scored his second in the final minutes, pouncing on loose play by the Lions to intercept the ball and outpace Quan Horn to touch down next to the right-hand post. Quan Horn: He’s already appeared for the Springboks on a couple of occasions, and if he continues to play like that, he will certainly play for them again. Despite the Lions being on the back foot for most of the game, he showed signs of sheer electricity on the attack, giving the Lions some real go-forward ball. Although he was turned over a couple of times, and lost in a foot race to Ioane, he showed real promise against a tough opposition. Ethan Blackadder: He certainly played his way back into Test contention with this performance. The Crusaders back-rower was superb in the breakdown, made some splendid runs while always looking for the supporting runner. He was rewarded for his persistence midway through the second half, when he showed excellent pace to race over the Lions try-line. The only negative: his left-handed passing is suspect. Timoci Tavatavanawa: A brilliant running display at inside centre, beating eight defenders, making three line breaks, and running 138 metres. His low centre of gravity and exceptional leg drive made him a nightmare to deal with, plus his teamwork was excellent, making a team high of four offloads. Even without the ball, he was terrific, making two turnovers and running excellent dummy lines. The Highlanders star has but a handful of All Black caps to his name, but if he continues to play like that, then Dave Rennie will surely start to issue him more. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. Sir Steve Hansen: All Blacks ‘in a position to win it’ but must ‘get desperate’ against Springboks in Cape Town Lions fatigue: A long European season for the URC side showed in the latter stages of the game, when the previously energetic Lions started to make mistakes. Although they fought hard, lapses of concentration eventually caused their downfall, with their previously comprehensive lead being chipped away until there was nothing left in the tank. Beauden Barrett: He didn’t play badly; he was just very unfortunate. A one-handed catch-and-kick ended up in a knock-on; an offload from Ioane didn’t quite go to hand, and he spent a fair proportion of his day on clean-up duty. All very frustrating, considering the 147-cap playmaker will have been desperate to impress as he sees his teammates take to the field on Saturday. All Blacks indiscipline: They conceded eight penalties overall, and each one hurt them. Lions star Chris Smith’s boot was enough to turn a promising attacking position into devastating losses, as the visitors suffered from their overeagerness. Noah Hotham: He was slow around the breakdown, giving Mo’unga leisurely ball which didn’t help with the early Lions onslaught. This all came after his first box-kick went straight into touch, from which he never really recovered. He’s inexperienced, which certainly explained the intercept pass to Mahashe, but he’ll be unlikely to see another black shirt for a while. Batho Hlekani: Smashed in his first contact and knocked the ball on in his second catch attempt, before then being knocked backwards in his third big attempt at a charge. title: WHAT COMES TO MIND … v SPY v SPY AND NOT FEARING THE GOOD - bernardzuel.net
content: Here we have the next instalment in What Comes To Mind, an alternative series in the Wind Back Wednesday space, based on the work of the brilliant photographer Stuart Spence, whose not-so-secret goal was to dig into my brain or soul or what might pass for both. Each time, he pulls out a photo from his archives going back almost 50 years and challenges me to respond with what comes to mind when I look at that image. It might be serious or ridiculous, personal or historical, but it will be inspired by a photo I’ve not seen before, and maybe even unseen by anyone beyond Stuart himself. This week, v Spy v Spy - captured here as I remember them: always moving, always passionate, always dressed ready for battle - lead us into something existential in any career. ___________________________ BEING THE BEST is presumed to be the goal of anyone in all fields: sport, arts, politics, or the hugely competitive world of country bakeries, each declaring with no shortage of chutzpah – hey, this isn’t some Tidy Town competition; this is serious – that they host the most famous/most loved/most sold pies in Australia. And who is going to argue with them? Not me, with my mouth full of their product. For scientific research purposes, of course. And anyway, they take it too personally or professionally to countenance an argument. If you’re not the best, however you want to measure that, there is no point it seemed. What about, for your public-facing career, being good or being long-lasting at being good? You know, offering a solid contribution through a long period even if no one says you’re the best or maybe never reaching heights that removed doubt but gee, no one was complaining either. Or maybe you toured with Midnight Oil and opened for INXS but never sold as much as them. Your songs might spark a good memory if heard on a classic Oz rock station but wouldn’t cause a flood of calls demanding you be added to their playlists to refresh that memory. Something like v Spy v Spy, a band that has been around since 1981 on and off (on for about a decade, mostly off for another decade or so, then on in various, sometimes contentious arrangements for the past two decades) and who could probably trigger recognition if you heard them pass by on the radio without necessarily bringing forth the name of many songs straight away. They weren’t first rank stars, they didn’t smash through – though you’ll still hear me playing their Do What You Say single, Four Fresh Lemons EP, & Harry’s Reasons album on occasion – but they did what they were trying to do, make music, they did more than survive and they did it long enough to feud, long enough to threaten a court case or two and lose one member to ill health, long enough to reform, remind and rekindle. Recently I was reading some typically frank posts by Canadian singer/songwriter Ron Sexsmith in which he spun tales of how various albums came together, how the photos were chosen for the cover, how the promises slipped away sometimes, and how the love came through sometimes too. His musings mixed a reasonable serving of the sang-froid that comes from a career that’s given him four decades of getting heard and respected by a not-unreasonable number of people with a touch of the bitterness that comes from battling for four decades to be heard and respected by more than a not-unreasonable number of people. What struck me about his posts was something similar to a conversation I had with him a few years ago, where it became clear that good was the enemy of imperfection. That is, the fact that Ron had made so many good albums – and dotted among them often enough, some great records – was almost a given, but rather than a boon this perversely meant the absence of terrible ones undermined the media value overall of his work. Why? Reviewers would note, as I did, that we were often looking for different ways of saying “this is another good Ron Sexsmith record” in ways that couldn’t help but sound like we wished, just for variety, to be able to say, “ah thank god, he’s made a shit one and I’ve got a lot to say about that”, possibly to be followed in a few years by some “return to form” headlines and reviews. The problem with this is consequently, less was said, if anything was said at all, about yet another good record because it wasn’t a “great” one or, indeed, a “terrible” one. Which is, as I said, perverse. But not uncommon. We are told often enough that if you’re not striving for, or if you fall short of, whatever is judged the real or proper measure of success then you’re a failure and who wants to be, or accept, failure? Losers, obviously. Silver medal? First loser. Non-prize winner? Regular loser. Declining to take the career-ladder route? Someone who is embedding losing in perpetuity. Just ask the then editor of the Sydney Morning Herald some years back who called me into his office to discuss career opportunities (not out of some personal concern; more stamping his authority on the place as he was relatively new to the job and probably had read this is how management worked). Where did I, arts writer/music specialist, see myself in five years, he asked me, almost pro forma as I guess he thought the answer would be. Doing this job but doing it better, was the response that came without much contemplation – not because I hadn’t given it any thought but because I had given it a lot of thought for a long time and it was so obvious I didn’t hesitate. But wait, what about becoming a mid-level editor, then a correspondent or major roundsman, working my way up through management to senior editing eventually (“like me”, was the unspoken bit)? Changing companies and returning when headhunted, maybe to move on again at some point, chasing prestige as well as the cash? No thanks. So, I just wanted to stay in pretty much the same job? That is the level of my ambition? Yep, if all goes well I would become a better writer and keep getting better at the only newspaper I’d wanted to write for. I was a writer, had only wanted to be a writer, and management meant less and less, and finally no, writing. And where was the fun in that? As v Spy v Spy once put it, “you were advertising something you didn’t have”. His expression was priceless – well, actually, as I would find out, there was a price, but that would be later – and he sent me off saying he was disappointed in my lack of ambition. Something he repeated, though with less politeness, to one of the editors I reported to. The man wasn’t an arsehole; he was a decent bloke who would do some really good work for years to come, though not as an editor in a nice bit of aptness that did bring to mind another line from that same Spy song “you seem to talk about it so much, why don’t you do what you say?”. But in his eyes if you weren’t going to be a winner on his terms – moving up, playing the game, going for better than good, being the best – you were in effect, a loser. Catch What Comes To Mind on the road this weekend at Headland Theatre, Tathra Hotel, where on Saturday, Stuart Spence and Bernard Zuel will be showing some photos, swapping stories and offering some prizes tied to Australian music of the 1980s(ish). That will be followed by a band hitting some of those favourite songs, then a screening of that classic work of indie Australian alternative lives in Haydn Keenan’s Going Down, topped off with a Q&A with the film’s star, Tracy Mann. title: Hello, Dolly: V Explores Dolly Parton’s Most Iconic Looks From Her Archive - V Magazine
content: Dolly Parton stormed Nashville in 1964 and the world has never been the same. Back in 2015, country’s most glamorous icon gave V a special look at her personal archive for the very first time Dolly Parton stormed Nashville in 1964 and the world has never been the same. Back in 2015, country’s most glamorous icon gave V a special look at her personal archive for the very first time Fifty years after she first came to Nashville from the Smoky Mountains of East Tennessee, Dolly Parton celebrated her legacy in typically heartfelt style. This past December, Parton’s Dollywood Foundation joined forces with Chandelier Creative for a rare exhibition of select costumes that Parton wore throughout her colorful career. After sending her most emblematic ensembles to New York, Parton and friends transformed an industrial Chelsea space into a glittering wonderland, and hosted a fundraiser to benefit Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library. Along with an exhibition of the clothing, the evening featured a silent auction, video clips from Dolly’s greatest onstage moments, and performances by Rufus Wainwright, Jake Shears, and surprise guest Kylie Minogue. As part of the auction, photographer Dan Forbes was given unprecedented access to the country icon’s archive to shoot her clothing and accessories, shown here. It might, in Parton’s famous words, cost “a lot of money to look this cheap,” but if the money raised for the Library – Parton’s nonprofit devoted to providing books for underprivileged Tennessee children – is any indication, the legend’s splurges were well worth it. title: Steichen says Anthony Richardson will start vs. Lions in preseason - Colts Wire
content: On Tuesday, head coach Shane Steichen revealed his plan for the Indianapolis Colts' starters and the quarterbacks in the team's preseason finale on Saturday against the Detroit Lions. The starters did not play in the first two preseason games, but most will see the field for a series or two on Saturday. "8-12 plays," Steichen said, via The Athletic's James Boyd. Excluded from this group, however, are Daniel Jones and Jonathan Taylor -- they will not play. Tyler Warren and Alec Pierce may not play either. Steichen said that Anthony Richardson will get the start and play for a quarter. Riley Leonard will then play the second quarter, while Easton Stick plays the second half. Richardson got the start in Week 1 against New England and played the entire first half. Compared to Leonard, he had the better outing, completing 11-of-14 passes for 145 yards. He did, however, throw an interception that went through the receiver's hands and put the ball on the ground. In Week 2 against Atlanta, it was Leonard who got the start, and both he and Richardson struggled, as did the play around them. This preseason, Richardson is 14-of-23 passing for 169 yards with an interception. He's also rushed for 69 yards and a score. Leonard is 17-of-35 passing for 151 yards with an interception. From the outside looking in, it's difficult to gauge where this competition for the backup role is at. As Steichen acknowledged last week, each quarterback has flashed, but also had their ups and downs. That said, in preseason games anyway, Richardson's ability to extend plays outside the pocket has seemed to be a differentiator for him, helping to turn negative plays into positive ones, while keeping the chains moving. Saturday's preseason game will be the final data point for Steichen before a decision is made.

title: Gerritsen v. City of Los Angeles - Becket — Religious Liberty for All
content: As the historic heart of the City of Los Angeles, El Pueblo Historical Monument draws millions each year to its Olvera Street market, historic buildings, and cultural celebrations rooted in the area’s unique Mexican-American heritage. But now a local resident is suing to tear down two longstanding features of El Pueblo—a cross erected in 1929 to commemorate Los Angeles’s founding and a nativity displayed each Christmas —because he is offended by their religious nature. El Pueblo de Los Angeles marks the birthplace of the City of Los Angeles. It sits near the site where Los Pobladores—the original 48 settlers who came from the Sonora and Sinaloa regions of New Spain (now Mexico)—built the original settlement that would grow into Los Angeles. Today, El Pueblo has been preserved as a state historic park and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Every year, more than two million people visit El Pueblo to tour the historic buildings, enjoy Mexican food, and shop for traditional crafts sold in the small shops that run through Olvera Street. The effort to preserve El Pueblo began in the late 1920s, when Olvera Street and many surrounding landmarks had fallen into disrepair. As part of the preservation effort, a 10-foot hand-carved wooden cross was erected at the head of Olvera Street in 1929 to commemorate Los Angeles’s 148th birthday. The Olvera Street market was also created, selling Mexican goods to celebrate the area’s rich historic past. The market allowed many members of Los Angeles’s Mexican-American community to launch successful businesses as Olvera Street merchants, even amid the Great Depression. Generations of merchants keep Olvera Street’s traditions alive Since El Pueblo’s revitalization in the 1920s, Olvera Street merchants have played a vital role in preserving and promoting the area—and drawing visitors to enjoy the city’s most historic district. Many of today’s merchants come from families that have been part of Olvera Street since the market opened in 1930. Together, they carry on longstanding cultural traditions through the Olvera Street Merchants Association Foundation. Throughout the year, the merchants help organize celebrations including Día de los Reyes, Cinco de Mayo, Día de losMuertos, and Las Posadas. Each December, a life-size nativity stands in the gazebo at the center of the Old Plaza as part of traditional celebrations of Christmas. In 2025, a local resident sued the City of Los Angeles, saying the cross and nativity offended him and made him feel excluded. He asked a federal court to remove or cover the cross and stop displaying the nativity. The district court rejected his request, finding that both displays are constitutional under the Establishment Clause because of their longstanding place in our nation’s history and traditions. With Becket’s help, the Olvera Street Merchants Association Foundation is asking to join the case and defend El Pueblo’s Mexican-American traditions, which its members have spent generations preserving. The cross has commemorated Los Angeles’s founding for nearly a century, and the nativity is part of the neighborhood’s longstanding celebration of Las Posadas. Becket is asking the court to make clear that the First Amendment does not require cities to erase such religious symbols and traditions from public life simply because someone takes offense to them. title: Marquette names V. Clayton Lafferty Endowed Chair in Electrical Engineering - Marquette Today
content: Following a nationwide search, Marquette has named Dr. Payman Zarkesh-Ha as the Opus College of Engineering’s V. Clayton Lafferty Endowed Chair in Electrical Engineering and professor of electrical and computer engineering. Zarkesh-Ha previously served as professor of electrical and computer engineering at the University of New Mexico, where he also held the position of Director of the Center for High Technology Materials. His research focuses on microelectronics and VLSI system design and modeling. He has published over 140 peer-reviewed journal papers and conference proceedings, and he holds 23 U.S. patents in his field. The V. Clayton Lafferty Endowed Chair in Electrical Engineering was established in the Opus College in 2011 to support education and research in smart sensor systems. The position is named in honor of V. Clayton (“Clay”) and Beverly Lafferty, 1950 graduates of the university’s Opus College of Engineering and Klingler College of Arts and Sciences, respectively. Clay Lafferty spent much of his professional career as the head of research and development at United Parcel Service. He held several patents and created the hub system used to support the company’s package delivery and logistics business. A legacy family with multiple generations having graduated from Marquette, several members continue to support student success and research initiatives in the Opus College. “Dr. Payman Zarkesh-Ha will bring world-class expertise to Marquette and Milwaukee, continuing to define our university as a hub of education and innovation in sensor technology and microelectronics,” said Dr. Kristina Ropella, Opus Dean of the Opus College of Engineering. “We are grateful to the Lafferty family’s support and vision for Marquette’s educational and research missions. Their generosity paves the way for Marquette engineers to develop novel solutions to serve communities.” At Marquette, Zarkesh-Ha will lead research in the university’s advanced microelectronics and sensors lab and class-1000 cleanroom. He will teach undergraduate and graduate courses in advanced analog electronics this fall, and several courses in the future in the areas of microelectronics, device fabrication and VLSI. title: Newcastle v West Brom | Carabao Cup 2nd Round Tie | Match Preview - Yahoo Sports
content: Newcastle United begin their 2026/27 Carabao Cup campaign on Wednesday evening when West Bromwich Albion make the trip to St James' Park for a second-round tie under the lights. The match, scheduled for Wednesday, August 26, with a 7:45pm kick-off, gives Matthias Jaissle his first opportunity to lead Newcastle into the competition as head coach. For the Magpies, the Carabao Cup represents an important opportunity to build momentum during what is a new era at the club. Newcastle have enjoyed an impressive record in this competition in recent seasons, winning the trophy in 2025, while also reaching the final, semi-final and quarter-final across the last four campaigns. There is therefore an expectation that Newcastle will take the competition seriously, even with Premier League fixtures coming thick and fast. The timing of the tie is particularly interesting. Newcastle are coming off an entertaining 2-2 draw against Liverpool at St James' Park, a match in which the hosts looked on course for a famous opening-day victory before a stoppage-time penalty rescued a point for the visitors. With Tottenham Hotspur awaiting Newcastle at the weekend, Jaissle may be tempted to rotate his squad, giving opportunities to players who need minutes while protecting some of his key first-team regulars. That rotation could make this a fascinating test of Newcastle's squad depth. West Brom, meanwhile, arrive on Tyneside in excellent spirits. The Baggies have made a perfect start to their competitive campaign, winning their Carabao Cup opener against Rotherham United 4-1 before recording Championship victories over Norwich City and Burnley. Their 3-1 victory over Burnley at the weekend will have further boosted confidence ahead of what is undoubtedly their toughest fixture so far. West Brom have already demonstrated that they are capable of scoring goals, and Newcastle will need to ensure that any changes to the starting XI do not affect their defensive organisation. The visitors will also see the occasion as an opportunity to test themselves against Premier League opposition at one of English football's most famous stadiums. The last meeting between the two sides at St James' Park came back in December 2020, when Newcastle claimed a 2-1 Premier League victory. West Brom's upcoming visit will therefore be their first to the stadium in almost six years. One of the biggest questions surrounding Wednesday's match will be how much Jaissle changes his side. Cup competitions traditionally provide opportunities for fringe players and youngsters, and Newcastle have plenty of players who will be eager to impress the new head coach. For those players, this is about more than simply progressing into the third round. A strong performance could influence their chances of featuring more regularly in the Premier League. Newcastle will go into the contest as favourites, particularly with home advantage behind them, but West Brom's perfect competitive start means this should not be treated as a straightforward assignment. The atmosphere under the St James' Park lights should provide another intriguing chapter in Jaissle's early Newcastle tenure. A victory would secure progression into the third round, maintain the club's strong recent record in the competition and, perhaps most importantly, give several players the chance to make their case to the new head coach. For Newcastle, the message is simple: respect the opposition, take the opportunity seriously and get the job done.

(03:08:40)The second possible explanation was as part of an attempt to take one's own life as part of a suicide, one might harm one's children if you thought that would prevent them from suffering. And let me see if I can give you an example of that. If one of us were to learn and we had no doubt in our mind that the Holocaust was coming tomorrow, and we thought that was going to be awful and I can't live through that and so I'm going to take my own life. If I had children, the question might come up, do I take them with me? Do I take their lives as well? Now, I'm not saying that I would definitely do that, but what I'm saying is that it would come up as a possibility in what I thought about. And so there ended up being, in my mind, two possible explanations for why she did what she did. (03:09:51)The first being the acute psychosis with command hallucinations. And the second being this was a serious suicide attempt and she wanted the children to be with her so she wouldn't be separated from them and so they wouldn't have to suffer after she was gone. Now in a minute, I'm going to talk about the evidence that I saw supporting each of those. But I will tell you right now in advance of talking about that, that most of the evidence that I saw supported the second one and not the first. And so doctor, if we could go to the next slide and you could talk to us, tell us what evidence you saw for acute psychosis with command hallucinations. Yes. The first was that's what she said. I asked her that question and that's the way she explained it happened. She said sometime on the afternoon of January 24th, 2023, that she heard a voice and the voice said, "This is your last chance. You have to kill the kids so you can kill yourself." If she actually heard a voice like that, that would be evidence of psychosis being experienced and what we call command hallucinations where the voice is instructing her to do something. There were some other possible things that made me think that it could be a severe mental illness that she was experiencing and two in particular. One was thinking that others might know her thoughts. Now, this is something that is a symptom of psychosis called thought broadcasting if it's experienced in a certain way. In thought broadcasting, if I'm experiencing that, I literally have the idea that if I'm thinking it, you can hear what I'm saying just as if I were putting it on the television or a podcast or a movie or whatever. It's just coming out that way. (03:12:17)I asked her about that and other people ask her about that too and she said it was not thought broadcasting, but these were very vivid thoughts. And she thought that it might be that people could hear them as vivid and strong as they were. The second possible symptom is that thinking police might take her children. Now, in some of the records I saw people saying, well, this looks like a paranoid delusion to me. And I will tell you that it didn't look either paranoid or like a delusion to me. And here's why. I'm a healthcare professional. And that means that in Pennsylvania and every other state I know, I'm a mandated reporter. If someone tells me in therapy or in an assessment that they think that a child is going to be injured or severely hurt or that might happen, then I'm required by law to contact child line in Pennsylvania. Ms. Clancy is a labor and delivery nurse. She's a healthcare professional as well. And so it's one of those things where if she had said to a psychiatrist, psychologist, anyone providing treatment that she thought she was experiencing ideas like she might harm her kids, she would know as a mandated reporter that they were legally required to report that. Now that might not mean that the police would literally come and take her kids away, but it would mean that there would be an investigation. She would have to answer questions. And it might be that for a period of time she would be separated from the children. I just want to ask a follow-up question about your last point. Is that okay? And so you mentioned you didn't think it was a delusion. Is it true that a delusion is a fixed false belief? And so Ms. Clancy, thinking that if someone knew she thought of harming her kids, her kids might be taken away, that's not a false belief, correct? Well, that was what I was trying to say is that it is not a false belief. It's quite possible that it could come to pass. Okay. And if you could continue with your discussion of the evidence you saw for acute psychosis. Yes. The other point there at the bottom is that it's appealing as an explanation because it could explain acts that seem so out of character for her. You don't have to get complicated at all. It's just, I had a psychotic episode, I heard a voice, voice told me to do something terrible, I did it. And after considering the evidence for acute psychosis command hallucinations, did you then consider evidence against acute psychosis with command hallucinations? One of the reasons, well, the first bullet point here is that the way she described this as happening is that she heard a voice that she'd never heard before, experienced an hallucination. And she's never experienced it since, but she only experienced it for the 18 minutes or so that it took to kill the children. And to put it mildly, that would be a very, very unusual pattern or manifestation of how this kind of thing comes about. Very unusual. I've been doing this kind of evaluation for many, many years and I'm always very careful when someone tells me that they experienced a symptom only during the course of committing an offense. Why is that, doctor? Why are you careful when someone tells you that they only experience this voice during a criminal offense? Well, because it provides a convenient way of lessening your own culpability. I mean, it's always possible, but as I said, I find it very, very rare. Whereas an explanation for why somebody did something, somebody might look at that and say, it's a convenient way of somebody looks at me and I don't have the same culpability that I would otherwise. And what was the next part of evidence that you saw against acute psychosis? There was some discussion of whether this was postpartum. And so she was about eight months away from having given birth to Cowan, her youngest child. And most of the explanations or most of the sources of authority like DSM-5 or the Cleveland Clinic will point to maybe one month after birth or two months after birth or something like that. But the... Birth or two months after birth or something like that. But the farther away you get time-wise from the birth, the less likely it is under those kinds of authority to be postpartum. Now it could be something else. And there were certainly some things that I saw that were symptoms of depression and other sorts of things that she experienced in January, but it was given the time, it was less likely, I thought, to be postpartum. Then the next bullet was inconsistencies in her account. To me, when asked about this, she said the voice said, "This is your last chance. You have to kill the kids so you can kill yourself." And it just kept repeating that. And only that, and only that for about 18 minutes or the duration of the time it took to do this. (03:18:59)There were other times though, for instance, when she was in the hospital after this happened and was talking to a psychiatric attending, when she said that the voice had said other things, for example, "The children will suffer without you or you have to take the kids with you," or things like that. So inconsistency is important because it suggests inaccuracy. In other words, which version is accurate? Is it the first? Is it the second? Is it neither? I mean, here it couldn't be both because she said, "I only heard this," to some people she said that. And then, "I heard this, plus this," to other people; she said that. And Doctor, if she had said to a third person that it was a different version, such as, "You have to kill the kids so you can kill yourself because there's a danger to you and the kids," would that be a further consideration of the inconsistencies? So it's not based on evidence. It's a hypothetical. So if the person has a third version of what happened, what the voice said, and what the reasons the voice gave, would that be important in your assessment as well regarding inconsistency? Objection. It's speculation. It's not based on evidence, and there's no foundation for a hypothetical question. Just ask it as the hypothetical. Assuming this and go that way. Doctor, a hypothetical question for you. Assuming that a person has already given two versions of a voice, what the voice said for them to do, and then gives a third version of what the voice told them to do, would that be significant to you in assessing the inconsistencies? What I would say is the more inconsistency there is, the more problematic I find it to take any one particular account and say this is the accurate one. And then what other evidence did you find against acute psychosis? There is some research that's been conducted on malingered hallucinations, which are counts of hallucinations that are exaggerated or fabricated. And I found it useful to look at that research and see what it suggested and kind of laid out there in terms of the way she described it. So some research suggests that one consideration is whether the voices are internal or external, whether they're coming from your own thoughts or whether they're coming from outside of your head. And Ms. Clancy perceived this voice as external, which is more consistent with genuine hallucinations. However, command hallucinations are often in about 88% of individuals reporting them by one account, accompanied by a related delusion. (03:22:38)Ms. Clancy did not report any accompanied delusions. So thus far you've got one point for genuine and one point for possible exaggerated. Then there's frequency and control. Genuine psychotic hallucinations are more often intermittent than constant. They'll come and they'll go. You'll hear it. Stop hearing it. You'll hear it again. Stop hearing it. And this can extend over a period of time. Ms. Clancy, in this instance, reported that the voice was constant for 18 to 20 minutes, and then it stopped. It had not been experienced before, and it has not been experienced since. And she also did not report having any control over the voice or over her actions in response to the voice. (03:23:29)Then the next item is content. So genuine hallucinations are often familiar, use both genders, and are clear rather than vague. Ms. Clancy described this voice as clear, but it was unfamiliar and it was a single male voice. So that was sort of mixed. I'm not counting it as one direction or another. And then finally, reaction and coping. Individuals who experience hallucinations like this often try to reduce their influence in different ways. Could be praying, could be listening to music. And while those who inaccurately report the experience of such hallucinations often do not describe coping mechanisms. And Ms. Clancy didn't report any attempt to stop the voice or distract herself from it or what have you. So there were about three points on which her account more closely resembled exaggerated or fabricated hallucinations. One where it looked more genuine and one that was kind of mixed. If I could ask you a question, you said that there were more points indicating malingering or exaggerating the existence of the voice. But earlier you testified about your psychological testing of Ms. Clancy, and it showed minimization, and it didn't show malingering. Could you explain how those two things could occur in the same person at the same time? Yes. When we try to appraise through testing or specialized measures something that looks like malingering or exaggeration, the way we typically do it as psychologists who develop the measures is it looks like somebody who is going to take a shotgun approach. They're going to say unusual things are wrong and strange things are wrong and many things are wrong and things like that. If you do that, we're pretty good at picking up that shotgun approach to malingering. But if I ask you a bunch of questions and you answer them almost entirely in a genuine way, that you're being as accurate as you can, except with one exception, when I ask you about one experience or one symptom and you exaggerate or fabricate that, we can't pick that up through our testing. So what we have to do instead is we have to kind of develop our ideas about how it might have been experienced, what it was consistent with what the disorder is. We take a broader approach, which is what I've tried to do in talking about this. We'll go to the next slide, please. And was there further evidence against acute psychosis? Yes. I'm going to start with the question of thoughts or hallucinations. I've already said that I found the account of hallucinations to be, as she described it, it would be very, very unusual to experience it that way. Never having not before, not since, constantly for 18 minutes. However, if this was a thought, an unwelcome, intrusive thought, but still a thought, that's basically, "This is your last chance. You have to kill the kids so you can kill yourself." Then that would be consistent with thoughts that she'd been experiencing for some time. She'd been having thoughts about harming herself, that it was going to be very difficult for her to do this in a way that made sense. (03:27:29)She was experiencing thoughts about hurting herself because her brain might have been damaged. She was experiencing thoughts about hurting the kids. She was experiencing all sorts of unwelcome thoughts. If that were the case on January 24th, if these were thoughts, then that would be consistent with what she'd been experiencing for months before. So that was something that made more sense to me: that rather than an auditory hallucination, it would have been an unwelcome, intrusive thought. The next bullet is her response to her husband's question, "What did you do?" So when he got home around 6:00 PM on January 24th and the house was quiet and he went in, thought people might've been playing hide-and-seek with him. Called downstairs, didn't get an answer. Called upstairs, didn't get an answer. Went upstairs, found the bedroom door locked, unlocked it with his key, went in, saw some blood there, saw the window was open, ran downstairs, and he saw his wife, Lindsay, lying there semi-conscious. (03:28:55)And he said his first question was, "What did you do?" And her response was, "I tried to kill myself." Now, I thought that if she had actually experienced this command hallucination, that she might've said something like, "I did what I had to do. I did what the voice said," or something like that. But no, she said, "I tried to kill myself." And this is consistent with my looking at this and starting from the perspective of this is a serious, highly lethal suicide attempt. And that's the way to understand it. And then the last bullet point has to do with the recovery of memories. So when she regained consciousness that night in the hospital, one of the things she said is that she wasn't able to remember what had happened. And she was informed of it. But if this had been genuine memory loss, then human memory is funny. (03:30:08)And one of the things that happens is that when you're trying to remember something that actually happened, things can interfere with that. Things that you read, things that you're told, other sorts of things like that. So it would have been hard to understand how she would recover that memory accurately, including the particular memory of the command auditory hallucination and what it said. And Doctor, did you already go over the first bullet point, the inconsistencies in her description of knowing wrongfulness? Yeah. I'm going to pass on that one and go to the next slide. Well, there were some additional inconsistencies in terms of whether she knew that... When I asked her whether she was aware that it was illegal or immoral, she said basically, "I wasn't thinking about this at all. No thoughts, no decisions, none of that. It was just all action." One of the things that Dr. Resnick wrote in his report is that she was intellectually aware that it was wrong or illegal but not morally. And what she said to me is that "I wasn't thinking about that at all. I didn't know any of that." Okay. And if we could go to the next slide, I think if you could describe for us the evidence that you saw for suicide combined with altruistic filicide. Yeah. "Altruistic filicide" is a term that's used that means killing your kids out of love. Not because you're trying to be cruel or for material gain or because you want them out of your lives or any of that, but killing them out of love so that you could... Basically, they wouldn't have to suffer, so you could prevent their suffering. And what she did, I thought, was begin with what I said a minute ago was a highly lethal and very serious suicide attempt. It was preceded by months of thoughts and impulses about "You should harm yourself, you should kill yourself, your brain is damaged," that sort of thing. And that I think is the beginning of the way to understand what happened that day. The second point is that, as I've said before, she didn't like to leave her children. Whether that was for date night or school or going back to work or anything, she did not like to leave her children. And if she had taken her own life, then her children would have been without her, and she thought that they would suffer. And she'd been having these thoughts, both about herself and about her children, over a several-month period. And the other thing that I will say is that she was in pain. She was suffering. She was doing a little bit better than she had been before she went into McLean, but she was still in pain. (03:33:43)She was suffering. I think she was even desperate. And that is something that is often characterized as people who try to take their own life. They're in pain, they're suffering, and they're trying to put a stop to it. And I think when she decided at some point that she was going to put a stop to it, then she had to answer the question of what to do about the kids. And she didn't want to leave them. And she was convinced that they would suffer without her. Go to the next slide. And further evidence that you saw for the suicide combined with altruistic filicide? There was. One of the things that she said when asked about what happened is that in the course of strangling each child, she said, "Go to God, baby. Go to God." And that was part of her expectation that she and the children would be together in heaven with God. She was raised as a Catholic. And this, as I understand, Catholic considerations; that's not necessarily what happens. But when I asked her about that, when I said, "Isn't suicide a mortal sin?" Yeah. Can I see counsel over here? All right. And so I'm going to ask you to go back to the jury room and then we'll bring you back in a couple of minutes. All right? Court, all rise. Jurors [inaudible 03:36:03], please. This way. (03:36:03)Jurors are next to the court. This court's in session. All right. We'll be in a short recess, and I'll come out as soon as I can. (03:36:41)This court is back in session. Please be seated. Your Honor, for the purpose of the record, we return back to the trial of Commonwealth vs. Lindsay Clancy. All parties are present, excluding the jury. All right. After the following sidebar conference, I think the defendant made a motion. I'm going to allow an argument in regards to the motion. I'll hear first from the defendant, and then I will hear from the Commonwealth. Mr. Reddington. Thank you, Judge. Your Honor, this has been obviously a long trial and a lot of work on the part of everybody involved, from the court to the staff, to the prosecutors, to myself. And needless to say, the strain on Lindsay Clancy. I have to move for a mistrial reluctantly. The reason is that this is intentional misconduct on the part of the prosecution. You know that this whole idea of injecting Roman Catholic faith, the concept of mortal sin, into this trial occurred, I don't even remember now, about a week ago. And I objected, but before I could get the objection out, Your Honor had us at the sidebar at the same time and very forcefully, in my opinion, indicated to the jurors that they should not consider that to any degree. At the time, I put on record the fact that I did not feel that... (03:38:10)I felt that the court's instructions were sufficient. They were forceful. They were right on point. And we moved forward without a motion for a mistrial. I made a tactical decision. But unfortunately at this point, it's a concern I have because this is just over the top. It's the same thing again: talking about religion, talking about heaven, talking about killing people and the impact of the effect that it would have on Lindsay as well as her children. The fact that this is not the first time that it occurred during the trial and the prosecution has previously brought up the concept of mortal sin. Based on your ruling in the past, in conjunction with the fact that they brought it up again, I believe it was intentional misconduct. And I feel that the court should grant a motion for mistrial. Thank you, Your Honor. The question I asked the witness did not ask for any testimony about religion, about Catholicism, about mortal sins or anything like that. And the slide is still up on the screen. There's nothing on the slide about Catholicism, about mortal sins, about any of that. The witness was explaining his reasoning. I don't think it was intentional on the part of the witness either. If we look at his interview of Ms. Clancy, one of the things that this witness has to do is determine whether the defendant knew the wrongfulness of her conduct. And that can be either that it was criminally wrong or morally wrong. And he explored that with her in the interview and asked her about whether she knew it was legally wrong. And she said she had no concept of legal consequences. And then he went on to ask her about moral wrongfulness and about her religion and whether she knew it was morally wrong. (03:40:03)And she did say that she had knowledge that suicide was considered sinful. So I believe that's where the witness was going in trying to explain his reasoning. I don't think he was intentionally trying to inflame the jury or cause an issue in this case. I know I certainly wasn't because I didn't ask a question about her religion or a question that would invoke that kind of response. I asked him to explain what was on the slides and that's not on the slides. So there was no intentional conduct by the Commonwealth. That was not where I intended to go with this questioning. And I don't think that the witness intended to do any harm either. He was just explaining his rationale. So I would ask that the jury be instructed to disregard the answer, and I can speak to the witness and tell him not to talk about that reasoning for behind his thoughts, that he can testify about his conclusions, but to leave that portion of his reasoning out of his testimony. All right. Well, here's a concern I have is what the witness did say in regards to... He said, "Go to God, baby. Go to God." That was statements that had been made in evidence already. And then he indicated that was part of her expectation that she and the children would be together in heaven with God. All right. Now we're getting a little closer to a problematic area. Then he testified, "She was raised as a Catholic. And as I understand Catholic considerations, that's not necessarily what happens." How is any of that proper at this point? But it was not... (03:41:55)I'm not going to declare a mistrial at this time. What I am going to do is I'm going to bring the jury in. I'm going to tell him to disregard it. I'm going to tell him that's an inappropriate area of inquiry and that this witness's understanding of Catholic dogma or Catholic teaching is irrelevant. There's no evidence of his background or training or having been to the seminary or any of that. And that's where he injected that. And so I am giving that, but the Commonwealth, I'm going to strongly, in perhaps the strongest language, talk to him and let him know that he can't go into that. And then my thought is we're going to bring the jury back in. I'm going to give him that instruction, and I'm going to send him home. I don't want them leaving here today with the last thing they heard was a discussion about this witness's understanding of the Catholic teaching. (03:43:08)That's not the last thing they're going to hear. And so my thought is that as best I can, is to address that and minimize the damage or prejudice because I do presume that this jury will be able to follow those instructions. And so that would be my thought. We'll come back. That will give the Commonwealth plenty of time to talk to this witness, to let him know the areas that he should and should not go into. And then we can come back tomorrow and we can resume his direct examination and cross-examination. All right. So that'd be my thought. We'll bring the jury in. I'll give him that instruction, and then we will recess until tomorrow. Okay? Your Honor, just for the record, could I note that objection? Sure. Absolutely. All right. So are we ready for the jury? Yeah. Court, all rise. Jurors enter. This court's now in session. Please be seated. Your Honor, for the purpose of the record, we return back to the trial of Commonwealth vs. Lindsay Clancy. All parties are present, including the defendant and including the 18 jurors. All right. All right. Well, members of the jury, just before we broke, there was some testimony from that last witness. And I just want to give you some instructions in regards to that testimony. And I just wanted to let... The religion that the defendant was raised with is absolutely an inappropriate area of testimony. It is to be stricken. It is not to be considered. I can't be any more clear of that. It cannot be considered. Secondly, the witness's understanding of Catholic teachings and considerations, again, is immaterial; it's irrelevant; it is to be disregarded based on that testimony. All right? (03:46:26)And so because we had a little bit of a delay due to this, what I'm going to do is I'm going to excuse you until tomorrow. All right? And so the thought is we'll come in; we'll finish up with this witness. I believe the Commonwealth has another witness at that point, and then we'll talk about where we go. I apologize for any kind of confusion or delay, but I just wanted to make sure you had those instructions with you when you left here today. All right? So I'm sorry, but so I'll see you tomorrow. Thank you. Court, all rise. Jurors, be kind and close your notebooks and place them on the chairs. This way, please. Jurors have exited the courtroom. This court's in session. Please be seated. All right. Counsel, one more time. Can I see you at the sidebar? (03:47:58)All right. So we will be in recess until tomorrow. The anticipation is that the evidence will be done at some point tomorrow with the thought that most likely we'll have a charge conference sometime probably tomorrow afternoon, and arguments in charge would be on Wednesday. All right. Subject to change as they always are. So thank you, everybody, and we'll see you tomorrow morning. Thank you. Luckily for you, we deliver. Subscribe to our blog today.
